statement: In people who snort cocaine and have been diagnosed with cocaine-related destruction of the nose and palate (in the papers, cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions), the damage described ranges from a hole in the nasal septum, which nearly all of them had, to destruction of the turbinates, the side walls of the nose and the palate and, less often, of the walls of the eye socket and the skull base. How many people who snort cocaine develop such damage is not known, because every study read counted only people who already had it and had come to doctors; and whether the damage stops or heals after cocaine use stops has not been studied, since no series in the systematic review (published in 2022) and no paper read followed people after they stopped. In 17 retrospective case series published from 1989 to 2020 and gathered by a systematic review (127 people with these lesions among 282 participants; 61 men and 44 women, sex not given for 22; aged 22 to 66), the septum was involved in 126 people (99.2%), the inferior turbinate or the inner wall of the maxillary sinus in 75 (59%), the palate in 38 (29.9%), the ethmoid or the middle or superior turbinate in 29 (22.8%), and the thin bone between the nose and the eye socket (lamina papyracea), the eye socket itself or the skull base in 10 (7.9%) (Nitro et al., 2022, Table 4 and Figure 2; the abstract and results text give the 59% and the 29.9% to the nasal floor and the lower side wall instead, which leaves out the palate). These are counts at one time, added across series of which 12 (75 of the 127 people) studied people chosen for a particular site or presentation, such as a hole in the palate or a picture resembling vasculitis (editors' count from Table 2). Series from the same groups may share patients (three from one Italian group hold 53 of the 127; editors' count), which the review does not address, and for the Italian series of 2001 the review's counts mix clinical with imaging findings and include palatal holes and eye-socket infections that appeared only during follow-up (editors' comparison of the review's Table 3 with the primary paper). Changes to the outside of the nose, such as a sunken bridge (saddle nose, 7 people in 5 series) or a collapsed nose (7 people in 2 series by one team), were listed for 10 of the 17 series; the others did not report on the outside of the nose, so no share can be given. Where reported, people had used cocaine for 2 to 30 years; how long, how often and how much they had used, and whether they had stopped (known for 33 of the 127: 18 still using, 15 stopped; editors' count from Table 3), were too sparsely reported to relate to the damage. The review proposes that the damage starts at the septum and spreads to the lower, then the middle parts of the nose and only then to the eye socket and skull base; this is a hypothesis drawn from the counts, which the authors say needs prospective validation, describing the sparse data over time in one series (Trimarchi et al., 2003, not read) as seeming to fit it. Of 18 people seen in the otolaryngology department in Brescia, Italy, from 1991 to 1999 (10 men and 8 women aged 22 to 66; 17 admitted cocaine use at the first visit; followed for 12 to 108 months), all came with long-standing symptoms such as a blocked nose, nosebleeds or facial pain, and the commonest findings were widespread ulcers with dead tissue, extensive crusting and a hole in the septum; holes in the palate were present in 2 people at the first visit and appeared in 3 more during follow-up, with trouble swallowing and food or drink passing into the nose. On imaging at presentation (16 people), all had a septal hole, 12 had at least partial destruction of an inferior turbinate (both sides in 9), 10 of a middle turbinate, 2 erosion of the superior turbinates, 5 erosion of the side wall of the nose (reaching the lamina papyracea in 1) and 4 erosion of the floor of the nose, the hard palate; these counts come from the text and Table 3, because the paper's Figure 3 prints percentages that match neither (for example 61% for the inferior turbinate, against 12 of 16). During follow-up 2 people with severe destruction developed infections spreading from the nose into the eye socket and 1 a Staphylococcus aureus lung abscess, all of which cleared with antibiotics; 15 of 17 tested had S. aureus in the nose (Trimarchi et al., 2001). The papers explain the damage, without testing it and citing earlier work, mainly by cocaine narrowing the blood vessels of the nasal lining so that tissue dies, with possible parts played by substances mixed into the cocaine (such as levamisole; see the answer on levamisole), the force of the inhaled powder and repeated infection; milder changes (a stuffy nose, headache, a weaker sense of smell) are mentioned only as background in one paper, with no count of how often they occur. The damage can look like other diseases that destroy the middle of the face, among them granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis, a vasculitis), sarcoidosis and nasal lymphoma; older criteria described by the review suspected the condition when two of a septal hole, a palatal hole and destruction of the side wall were present, with other diagnoses ruled out and a drug screen (Seyer et al., as described by Nitro et al., 2022). The consensus panel's list of conditions to rule out also includes infections such as syphilis, leishmaniasis, leprosy and tuberculosis, Crohn's disease, long-term use of vessel-narrowing (decongestant) drugs, nose picking, injury, snorting other drugs and IgG4-related disease (Saibene et al., 2025, statement 2.3). In the Brescia comparison with all 21 people with Wegener granulomatosis and nasal involvement biopsied there in the same years, none of the 18 people with cocaine lesions had fever, weight loss, joint pain, or lung or ear involvement at presentation (13, 7, 7, 12 and 7 of the 21 had); markers of inflammation in the blood were lower on average (CRP 12.2 against 79.4 mg/L; ESR 31 against 66 mm/h), although CRP was abnormal in 9 and ESR in 8 of the 18, which the conclusion's statement that signs of systemic inflammation were absent in all does not fit; on imaging, the septum was perforated in 16 of 16 against 2 of 16, and structures beyond it were destroyed in 12 of 16 against none; routine ANCA blood tests, used to diagnose the vasculitis, were positive in 13 of 18 (19 of 21 in the comparison group), and some people with cocaine lesions were first treated as for the vasculitis, with cytotoxic drugs, without benefit; and in biopsies, changes in vessel walls were found in both diseases, but granulomas or giant cells (0 of 25 abnormal biopsies, against 9 of 22) and deep areas of dead tissue (0 of 25, against 19 of 22) only in the vasculitis. The authors say referral bias may explain part of these differences, since people with cocaine lesions may come to a doctor only after much damage. The consensus panel agreed that the diagnosis should not rest on autoantibody tests such as ANCA (statement 1.3, strong consensus) and defined the condition as any structural lesion of the nose and sinuses in a person whose cocaine snorting is confirmed by their own account or by a drug test (1.1, consensus, the lowest-rated statement adopted), a one-lesion definition it presents as replacing older ones. No series in the review reported what happened to the lesions after people stopped (use status was not reported for the one series with some data over time), and the only repeat imaging in the papers read is of 4 people in the Brescia series, all of whom said they had kept using cocaine and all of whom had further destruction on scans 7 to 52 months after the first; in one of them, over three years, it reached the whole framework of the nose, the hard and soft palate and the central floor of the front of the skull base, with brain tissue bulging through the gap (a meningoencephalocele). In the 2025 consensus (18 otolaryngologists under 45 from the rhinology research group of the young otolaryngologists' section of the International Federation of Otorhinolaryngological Societies, in five countries in Europe and North America, all of them authors, rating 44 statements from 1 to 9 over three anonymous rounds, rewording those short of consensus; strong consensus means a mean of at least 8 with no rating 2 or more points from it), the panel agreed that people with these lesions must be told that stopping snorting cocaine is the only known way to halt them (statement 3.3, strong consensus, mean 8.61) and that no 'safe threshold' of cocaine use keeps them from progressing (3.4, the highest-rated statement, mean 8.89), both supported in its discussion by a single cited paper (Trimarchi et al., 2014, not read); that repair of the septum, nose or palate should not be done unless the person is motivated and shows, by toxicology covering at least 12 months, that they have stopped (4.7, consensus, mean 8.61, one outlier), a period taken from the DSM-5 definition of sustained remission, with an uncited remark that the risk of relapse falls the longer abstinence lasts, rather than from any data on healing; that a plate covering the hole (an obturator prosthesis) can be offered first for a hole in the palate (3.15, consensus); and that lesions that grow after a person reports stopping call for a full workup for other causes, in which a drug test can be considered (2.13, strong consensus; 2.14, consensus). Repair techniques reached only near-consensus (4.8), the literature on them being described as anecdotal. The discussion describes a septal hole that has settled, with no crusting or inflammation, in someone who used cocaine in earlier years but not recently, as fitting cocaine damage, and crusting or inflammation then as a reason to look for another cause; no paper gives data on how often, or how fast, lesions settle, stay the same or grow after stopping. These statements are expert opinion: the panel's literature search kept only reviews and higher-level designs (23 articles, plus one the panel added), most of them, by the authors' account, descriptive studies without a control group; no statement carries a grade of its evidence; the review's first and senior authors were among the panel's three leaders, and the panel adopted the review's four-grade scale (statement 2.2); and only rhinologists voted, with no specialist in drug-use treatment and no person who uses cocaine, although the abstract calls the panel multidisciplinary. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: What does snorting cocaine do to the nose, and does it heal? In people who snort cocaine and develop this kind of damage, it ranges from a hole in the septum, the wall between the nostrils, to destruction of other parts of the nose, the roof of the mouth and, less often, the walls of the eye socket or the base of the skull. How many people who snort get it is not known: the studies counted only people who already had the damage and went to doctors. Among 127 such people in 17 published case series, 126 had a hole in the septum; about 59 in 100 had damage to the lower side walls of the nose, 30 in 100 to the roof of the mouth, 23 in 100 higher up in the nose and 8 in 100 reaching the eye socket or the skull base. Some had a sunken or collapsed nose; not every series reported on the outside of the nose, so how often is unknown. In one Italian clinic, 2 of 18 people developed infections that spread from the nose into the eye socket; antibiotics cleared them. The damage can look like a disease that inflames blood vessels: in that clinic, a blood test used to find that disease was positive in 13 of 18 people with cocaine damage, and some were first given treatment for that disease, which did not help. Unlike many people with the vessel disease, none of the 18 with cocaine damage had fever or illness elsewhere in the body, and certain features in tissue samples were found only in the vessel disease. Whether the damage stops or heals after stopping has not been studied: none of these studies followed people after they stopped. In the same clinic, 4 people were scanned again months or years later; all 4 had kept using cocaine and all had more damage, in one reaching the base of the skull within three years. A panel of 18 nose doctors agreed, as an opinion rather than a finding, that stopping is the only known way to halt the damage, that no amount of use is safe for it, and that surgery to repair it should wait until drug tests show 12 months without cocaine.
population: People who snort cocaine and have been diagnosed with cocaine-related destructive lesions of the nose or palate (cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions), as described in published case series: 127 people in 17 retrospective series published 1989–2020 (61 men, 44 women, sex not given for 22; aged 22 to 66), 12 series of which (75 people) selected people for a particular site or presentation; in the one primary series read, 18 people seen in 1991–1999 in one otolaryngology department in Brescia, Italy (10 men, 8 women; aged 22 to 66, median 37; 16 imaged), all tested for a vasculitis; and, for the expert statements, a panel of 18 otolaryngologists (rhinologists under 45) from five countries in Europe and North America
exposure: Snorting cocaine, as reported by the people themselves (17 of 18 in the Brescia series admitted it at the first visit; a reliable history of duration and amount could not be obtained for 7) or, in the consensus definition, shown by a drug test; where reported, 2 to 30 years of use; how often and how much people used, and whether they had stopped, were rarely reported and never related to the damage
comparator: None for the site counts (people with lesions only; no people who snort cocaine without lesions); in the Brescia series, all 21 consecutive people with Wegener granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) with nasal involvement biopsied in the same department and period (16 imaged); for the course of the lesions, repeat imaging in 4 people who kept using cocaine, and no one who had stopped
outcome: Which structures were perforated, eroded or destroyed (clinical examination, endoscopy, CT or MRI); changes to the outside of the nose; infections; features telling the lesions apart from the vasculitis (symptoms elsewhere in the body, blood tests including ANCA, imaging, biopsies); progression on repeat imaging; the panel's agreement (ratings from 1 to 9) on definition, diagnosis, repair and the course after stopping
magnitude: Nitro et al. (2022), 127 people with lesions in 17 series (Table 4; Fig. 2): septum 126 (99.2%); inferior turbinate or medial maxillary sinus wall 75 (59%); palate 38 (29.9%); ethmoid, middle or superior turbinate 29 (22.8%); lamina papyracea, orbit or skull base 10 (7.9%); counts per site, overlapping. Editors' Wilson 95% intervals treating the 127 as one sample, which overstates precision because the series were selected and differ: 95.7–99.9%, 50.4–67.2%, 22.6–38.4%, 16.4–30.9%, 4.3–13.9%. Series selecting a subgroup 12 of 17 (75 of 127 people); one group's three series 53 of 127 (editors' counts from Table 2). External nose (Table 5; 10 of 17 series): saddle nose 7 people in 5 series; nasal pyramid collapse 7 people in 2 series (editors' count). Use status known for 33 people: 18 using, 15 stopped (editors' count from Table 3); duration reported for 11 series (2–30 years), frequency for 2. Trimarchi et al. (2001), imaging at presentation, 16 of 18 people with lesions against 16 of 21 with Wegener granulomatosis (Table 3): septum 16 against 2; inferior turbinate 12 (both sides 9) against 0; middle turbinate 10 (both sides 5) against 0; superior turbinates 2; lateral nasal wall 5 (lamina papyracea 1); hard palate 4 (soft palate 1); 0 for each of these in the comparison group; second structure besides the septum 12 of 16 (75%) against 0 of 16; mean imaging score 4.06 (range 1–10) against 0.13 (0–1), p < 0.001. Figure 3 prints 61%, 33%, 16%, 11% and 28% for the inferior, middle and superior turbinates, the lateral wall and the floor or palate, which match neither. Palatal perforations 2 at the first visit, 5 by the end of follow-up (12–108 months, median 34). During follow-up: orbital infections 2, lung abscess 1, all resolved with antibiotics; S. aureus in the nose 15 of 17. Presentation, lesions against vasculitis (Table 1): fever 0 against 13; weight loss 0 against 7; arthralgia or arthritis 0 against 7; lung involvement 0 against 12; ear involvement 0 against 7; CRP 12.2 (SD 12) against 79.4 (73.7) mg/L, p = 0.002; ESR 31 (25) against 66 (41) mm/h, p = 0.009; abnormal CRP 9 of 18, ESR 8 of 18. Routine ANCA positive 13 of 18 against 19 of 21. Biopsies (Table 4): giant cells or granulomas 0 of 25 against 9 of 22; deep necrosis 0 of 25 against 19 of 22 (both p < 0.001); leukocytoclastic vasculitis 7 of 25 against 14 of 22 biopsies (p = 0.02), 6 of 18 against 9 of 21 people (printed p = 0.11; editors' Fisher exact p = 0.74). Repeat imaging: 4 people, 8 further examinations 7–52 months after the first, all still using, all progressed. Saibene et al. (2025), 18 panellists, ratings from 1 to 9 (mean; median; range; outliers; result): 1.1 definition 7.44; 7.5; 1–9; 1; consensus. 1.3 not relying on autoantibody tests 8.50; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 2.3 differential diagnoses 8.50; 9; 6–9; 1; consensus. 3.3 stopping the only known way to halt lesions 8.61; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 3.4 no safe threshold 8.89; 9; 8–9; 0; strong consensus. 4.7 repair only after toxicology-proven stopping covering at least 12 months 8.61; 9; 5–9; 1; consensus. 4.8 reconstruction techniques 7.94; 9; 4–9; 2; near-consensus. 3.15 palatal obturator first 8.11; 9; 3–9; 1; consensus. 2.13 full workup if lesions grow after reported stopping 8.56; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 2.14 drug test then 8.22; 9; 5–9; 1; consensus.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Background, with citations: snorting, often chronic and compulsive, causes repeated vasoconstriction that may lead to ischaemia and death of the nasal lining, followed after repeated exposures by damage to cartilage (the septum most often) and bone (hard palate, maxilla, anterior skull base), and to external deformities and life-threatening infections; the pattern mimics, and is often indistinguishable from, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis or nasal non-Hodgkin lymphoma. evidence.extracted: Background, with citations: habitual snorting may cause lesions of the lining; mild changes cause nasal stuffiness, headache or a reduced sense of smell; with chronic and compulsive use, progressive damage to the lining and the tissue covering the cartilage leads to ischaemic death of the septal cartilage and perforation; occasionally the bone and cartilage of the nose, sinuses and palate are extensively destroyed, mimicking other diseases with destructive lesions of the middle of the face. risk_of_bias.note: The site counts come from 17 retrospective case series chosen by their own authors, 12 of them (75 of 127 people) for a particular site or presentation, added together with no weighting or interval in a review rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_nitro_2022); one group's three series hold 53 of the 127 and may share patients, as may the two series by Colletti et al.; and the review's counts for the Brescia series mix clinical with imaging findings and findings at presentation with findings during follow-up. The Brescia series is a referral series of severe cases with unclear selection, imaging in 16 of 18 read by one radiologist and several statistical errors (JBI prevalence checklist, high; card sc_trimarchi_2001). These could change the shares materially (for example the palate share, in series chosen for palatal holes), but not the finding that the septum was involved in nearly everyone with these lesions: one level. The course after stopping rests on the absence of follow-up data and on the opinion of one panel of rhinologists (card sc_saibene_2025: the project's narrative-review checklist, high), which the statement reports as opinion, not as evidence of an effect.

inconsistency.note: Septal perforation is reported in nearly every person of every series (review Table 3). The shares differ between the Brescia series and the pooled counts (a middle turbinate destroyed in 10 of 16 imaged, against 29 of 127 for the ethmoid, middle or superior turbinate), as expected from the Brescia series' selection of severe cases considered for a vasculitis; the statement gives both.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the statement describes people already diagnosed with these lesions who had come to doctors, says that how often snorting cocaine leads to them is unknown, gives the course after stopping as unstudied and the panel's statements as opinion. A reader asking what snorting does to their own nose needs the missing denominator, which the plain lines name as the main catch.

imprecision.note: 127 people pooled without intervals (editors' Wilson intervals, which overstate precision because the series are not one sample: palate 22.6% to 38.4%; eye socket or skull base 4.3% to 13.9%), with the deeper sites resting on 10 to 38 people; the comparison with Wegener granulomatosis on 18 against 21 people (16 imaged in each group); progression on 4 re-imaged people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review, which excluded case reports because they tend to describe extreme cases; the selective publication of striking or site-specific series is part of the selection counted under risk of bias and is not counted twice.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (which structures were damaged in people already diagnosed, how the damage was told apart from a vasculitis in one series, what has and has not been studied about its course, and what one expert panel recommends): observational evidence starts low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low (the arithmetic floors at very low); descriptive claims are never upgraded. The certainty concerns the description of published cases. It does not extend to how often snorting cocaine damages the nose, which no paper read measured, or to healing after stopping, which no paper read studied. The panel's statements on stopping, the 'safe threshold' and the 12-month wait before repair are opinion (a consensus without patient data, its search excluding the primary case series) and are reported as such; resting on them alone, the claim would stay at draft. Status replicated: septal perforation in nearly every person is reported in each of the 17 series, by 14 different first authors (review Tables 2 and 3); but the shares come from one review whose pool includes the Brescia series and two later series from the same group, so they are not independently replicated, and the comparison with Wegener granulomatosis and the repeat imaging rest on one series. The review and the consensus share their first and senior authors and are not independent of each other. The claim gives no advice on use; amounts that people reported in the Brescia series are left out because no paper related them to the damage.
